title: Deutsche Bank Says India Can Be a Long-Term AI Winner
excerpt: artificial intelligence Deutsche Bank Says India Can Be a Long-Term AI Winner By Elets News Network - 23 November 2026. Share:. India could become one of the biggest long-term winners of the global artificial intelligence boom without building the world’s most advanced AI models, according to a new report by Deutsche Bank reported on 23 November 2026. The bank argues that India’s real opportunity lies in adopting existing AI tools at scale across its economy, rather than racing the United States and China on frontier models or chip manufacturing. The findings, first reported by The Economic Times , point to India’s population, digital public infrastructure and technology workforce as the factors that could turn AI adoption into broad productivity gains. Why Deutsche Bank sees India as an AI winner. The report says that the speed of AI adoption sets it apart from earlier technology waves. Steam power took about 80 years to reach lower-income countries, electricity about 40 years and the internet about 20 years. ChatGPT, by contrast, reached extensive usage in roughly six months. “You don’t need the latest AI model to enable millions of people and enterprises to become substantially more productive by giving them access to unprecedented amounts of tailored knowledge and skills at minimal cost. You don’t even need to invent it,” the report said. That framing matters for India, where policymakers have debated whether sovereignty in AI means owning frontier models or controlling the infrastructure and data on which they run. Recent moves such as the IndiaAI Mission’s release of Soket EKA-1 and ZenteiQ Dhir models show both tracks moving in parallel. Digital public infrastructure as the launchpad. Deutsche Bank highlights the base India has already built: affordable mobile data, smartphones, Aadhaar, Jan Dhan accounts and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). According to the report:. Internet access in India has risen from about 15 per cent to 70 per cent over the past decade. Bank account ownership has grown from slightly over half the population in 2014 to nearly 90 per cent today. India’s population is expected to reach 1. 5 billion by 2028, creating a very large market for AI-based services. The country produces roughly 11 million graduates a year, a deep talent pool for building and deploying AI applications. Because these rails already exist, the report says, businesses and government bodies can roll out AI services without building entirely new systems. Efforts such as Microsoft India’s AI chatbot for MSMEs are early examples of that layering approach. Sectors with the biggest AI upside. The report names banking, healthcare, education and agriculture as the sectors with the most to gain, given the large unmet demand for affordable services. In agriculture, for example, AI-enabled precision farming could help farmers forecast crop yields, spot pests and diseases early and improve farming practices. It also sees India emerging as a major global data centre hub, backed by investment from domestic business groups and international technology companies. That trend is already visible in deals such as L&T’s multi-year order for NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Chennai , though questions remain over how well new capacity is used, as a Rhodium Group analysis of India’s data centre boom noted earlier this month. What it means for Indian enterprises. For CIOs and technology leaders, the report reinforces a practical message: competitive advantage will come from deploying AI into real workflows, not from waiting for a homegrown frontier model. The dependence on foreign AI technology remains a risk, but Deutsche Bank’s view is that adoption at scale, built on India’s digital public infrastructure, is where most of the economic value will be created. Key takeaways. Deutsche Bank says India can be a long-term AI winner by adopting existing AI tools rather than building frontier models. title: The ECB warns of dependence on AI giants
excerpt: POLITICS & INSTITUTIONS - INSTITUTIONS. A risk in the making. The ECB warns of dependence on AI giants. Written by Thierry Labro. Published at 10:16 • Edited at 10:19. Share. The ECB recommends that financial institutions map their dependencies on AI and cloud providers, put in place fallback solutions across multiple providers and regions, and step up the monitoring of models and market risks. (Photo: Shutterstock). Artificial intelligence is making inroads into the banking and fund sectors, but is also concentrating their activities amongst a handful of US providers. Three days after launching a new survey of the financial sector, the ECB outlines how an IT failure or similar investment decisions could have a knock-on effect. A failure at a single provider can now affect banks, funds and their clients across several countries. The more artificial intelligence becomes embedded in the financial sector, the more common this single point of failure becomes. This is the main warning issued by the European Central Bank in its recently published Financial Stability Review. The institution does not yet regard AI as a systemic threat. However, it does see conditions emerging that could amplify a technical incident or a market correction. The issue has landed on the desks of Luxembourg’s financial professionals at the same time. Since 17 November, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier and the Banque Centrale du Luxembourg have been asking them to respond to a new survey on their use of AI. Banks, investment firms, payment institutions and authorised fund managers are affected. The questionnaire also covers specialised financial service providers (PSFs), support PSFs and crypto-asset service providers. Responses must be submitted to the supervisory authorities by 31 December. Publicité. Banks have changed in scale. In the eurozone, 86% of banks surveyed by the ECB were already using generative artificial intelligence in 2025. Just a year earlier, the figure stood at 46%. The technology is mainly used in IT operations, legal and regulatory services, and customer-facing activities. Applications likely to have a direct impact on risk remain less advanced. Artificial intelligence still plays a relatively minor role in risk management. Systems capable of planning and carrying out tasks autonomously – referred to as ‘agent-based’ AI – are generally still at the project or experimental stage. This rapid growth, however, shifts the focus of the question. It is no longer simply a matter of whether a bank or an asset manager uses AI. It is necessary to identify the infrastructure, models and providers on which its operations depend. Three companies – Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google – accounted for 82% of the European cloud market in 2025, according to estimates cited by the ECB. Together with OpenAI, they also controlled 90% of generative AI services. A failure on the part of any one of these stakeholders could therefore lead to similar errors or disruptions across several organisations. It could simultaneously affect customer service, fraud detection, compliance, IT development and, ultimately, risk management. The AWS outage on 20 October 2025 serves as a warning. Starting in a US cloud region, it disrupted services in more than 60 countries. Financial institutions accounted for only a small proportion of the reported incidents. But the incident demonstrated how a local failure could spread across sectors and borders. The ECB is not concerned that an outage of this nature would directly render banks insolvent. It fears that it would disrupt several critical services at once, undermine confidence and complicate the return to normality. Funds that could sell together. The other risk described by the ECB relates to investment decisions. How the RBI's API advisory and draft model risk guidance meet in a bank's third-party AI model
excerpt: . Vikram Raj Singh. Follow. Nov 20, 2026. 5 min Read. Fintech. BFSI. How the RBI's API advisory and draft model risk guidance meet in a bank's third-party AI model. A GenAI feature that an Indian bank builds on a third-party model can fall within two RBI documents at the same time, the 16 November 2026 advisory on API governance and security and the draft model risk management guidance dated June 2026. Reading them side by side, I would make two delivery decisions early. use the same model version identifier in the API audit trail and in the model change log, and put the model provider's retirement or shutdown date in the change plan from the start of the engagement. How the RBI's API advisory covers AI models. The RBI's advisory of 16 November on API governance and security covers, for the first time, APIs used to reach AI and machine learning models, according to Elets BFSI. The report says the RBI wants, among other things, access controls matched to each model's sensitivity, safeguards against prompt- or input-based misuse, and audit trails of model versions, administrative changes and relevant inputs and outputs. The record-keeping asked for in the RBI's draft model risk management guidance. The RBI's draft model risk guidance, dated June 2026, says the final guidance will follow public consultation (paragraph 64), and it sets out its own record-keeping requirements. It says no model should be used unless it is in the model inventory, which records, among other things, each model's owners, developers, validators and approvers (paragraphs 21 and 22), and it asks for a record of changes, versioning and approvals (paragraph 41). It asks for validation following modification of a model (paragraph 30), and says a breach of the threshold or criteria each regulated entity defines for a material change should re-initiate the process for validation and approval (paragraph 42). Why I would use one model version identifier in both records. In my reading, the overlap holds where the feature calls the third-party model through an API and meets the draft's definition of a model. For that case, my recommendation is to use the same model version identifier in the API audit trail and in the change log the draft describes, so a version change appears in both records with the same identifier. Why provider retirement dates belong in the change plan. The draft lists, for material third-party AI models, "changes in model behaviour or capabilities resulting from provider-driven updates" among the risks to consider (paragraph 53). Anthropic and OpenAI both publish dates after which older models stop accepting requests on the provider's own API, which Anthropic calls retirement and OpenAI calls shutdown, and both notify customers actively using a model in advance. I would put the provider's published retirement or shutdown date, or its earliest listed date, in the change plan from the start of the engagement. How I would split the statement of work for systems integrators. Both decisions need an owner, so for the statement of work, I would split the duties this way. The systems integrator building the feature would track the provider's notices, raise the change and supply the evidence pack. the API audit trail entries, test results on the bank's own prompts and the provider's notice. The bank would run the independent validation the draft asks for (paragraph 29). Who pays for that validation is worth agreeing in the contract at signing, because the retirement or shutdown date is set by whoever operates the model. Frequently asked questions. Nigeria’s Central Bank and the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) have called for stronger cybersecurity measures across financial institutions as the growing use of artificial intelligence creates new risks for digital payments, banking operations and customer information. Contents. How Is AI Increasing Cyber Risks? What Must Banks Change? Can AI Systems Be Trusted? Why Are Smaller Businesses Vulnerable? What Are the Regulatory Requirements? Why Does Human Behaviour Matter? The420 Insight. The warning was issued during the 2026 Cybersecurity Conference of the Information Security Society of Africa-Nigeria (ISSAN), where financial institutions were urged to strengthen security controls while adopting emerging technologies. How Is AI Increasing Cyber Risks?. Dr Rakiya Yusuf, Director of the Payments System Supervision Department at the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), said artificial intelligence was creating opportunities for financial institutions while introducing security challenges that required stronger safeguards. Yusuf, represented by Deputy Director Chika Ugwuze, explained that AI was increasingly being used to improve fraud detection, customer service and operational efficiency. However, cybercriminals could exploit the same technology to develop more sophisticated attacks against financial systems. She warned that traditional security measures, including firewalls and antivirus software, were no longer sufficient to address the growing complexity of cyber threats. What Must Banks Change?. Financial institutions were advised to adopt a broader approach to cybersecurity by integrating security considerations into daily operations, technology infrastructure and overall risk management. Yusuf emphasised that cybersecurity should no longer remain the responsibility of technology departments alone but should become a business risk requiring attention from institutional leadership and boards. She also urged organisations to strengthen their ability to assess, test and monitor emerging technologies before and after deployment. The objective is to ensure that technological innovation does not compromise security, operational resilience or accountability within the financial system. Can AI Systems Be Trusted?. NIBSS Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Premier Oiwoh, represented by Chief Information Security Officer Olusola Odediran, said financial institutions needed to carefully evaluate the risks associated with integrating AI into their operations. He stressed that automated systems required reliable data, appropriate safeguards and continued human oversight, particularly when supporting important financial decisions. Regular testing and monitoring were also necessary to maintain system reliability and prevent security failures. Why Are Smaller Businesses Vulnerable?. ISSAN President Dr David Isiavwe warned that cyberattacks posed a serious threat to business survival, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises. He stated that approximately 45 per cent of cyberattacks globally targeted smaller businesses and that at least 60 per cent of affected businesses failed to survive the consequences. These figures were presented as part of his warning about the financial and operational damage cyber incidents could cause. Isiavwe said increasing dependence on digital platforms had made cybersecurity a critical business concern rather than merely a technical issue. What Are the Regulatory Requirements?. title: Our strategy - built on trust, accelerated with AI | Views | HSBC Holdings plc
excerpt: . Our strategy - built on trust, accelerated with AI. By Georges Elhedery, Group CEO, HSBC. Topics. Explore topics related to Our strategy. 18 Nov 2026. Share. Email a link to this page. Banking is entering a new operating environment. Artificial intelligence is changing how customers make decisions, how businesses operate and how financial services are delivered. At HSBC, our colleagues are using AI to simplify processes, improve efficiency and create more personalised experiences. Payments, investing and treasury services are becoming faster, more intelligent and increasingly real time. Crucially, AI is beginning to accelerate delivery of our strategy and ambition, enabling us to move at pace and put customers at the heart of everything we do. Georges Elhedery, Group CEO, HSBC. We’re empowering relationship managers with AI to help them serve customers faster, while personalising the experience through more relevant support. As we reinvest productivity gains in our technology teams, we can bring forward delivery timelines - turning improved productivity into earlier outcomes and faster transformation. For customers, AI is reshaping how they engage with financial institutions: comparing products more quickly and exploring options more widely. However, customers and businesses continue to need the institutions - and the people - they trust to move capital safely, manage risk effectively and operate across borders with confidence. Particularly when complexity, risk and uncertainty are highest, customers want a trusted relationship: someone to challenge assumptions, provide context and apply judgement. In financial services, trust is built on expertise, judgement, conduct and accountability. These qualities matter most in an AI-enabled world. Technology can improve speed, analysis and efficiency, but financial decisions require insight, expertise and oversight. The organisations that succeed will combine innovation with trust, speed with discipline, and technology with human judgement. The AI opportunity. We see AI as an opportunity to become a simpler, more responsive and more connected bank for our customers and colleagues. Our vision is clear: to empower colleagues to use AI to create a personalised experience for each customer, deliver it safely, in real time and at scale, while keeping human judgement, decision-making and accountability at the core. We’re investing in the technology and platforms that strengthen how we serve customers, and giving colleagues the tools and training to adapt, succeed and benefit from the opportunities AI brings. We launched our AI Academy in October 2024 to build capability at scale. Open to all employees, it offers learning pathways from foundation to advanced, helping colleagues develop practical AI skills and use AI responsibly. Between January 2025 and September 2026, we’ve seen 585,000 hours of learning completed by 73,000 employees globally; that's an average of eight hours of training for every trained colleague. title: KI-Risiken könnten Versicherer an ihre Grenzen bringen
summary: Künstliche Intelligenz schafft nicht nur neue Risiken, sondern kann bestehende Gefahren erheblich verstärken. Eine gemeinsame Studie der Zurich Insurance Group und der Universität St. Gallen zeigt, weshalb solche Risiken für Versicherer zunehmend schwieriger kalkulierbar werden.
excerpt: Leben & Karriere. Fintech. Mediathek. English News. Middle East. Asia. Advertorials. Newsletter. Über uns. Werbung. Suche. Montag, 23. November 2026. KI-Risiken könnten Versicherer an ihre Grenzen bringen. Künstliche Intelligenz schafft nicht nur neue Risiken, sondern kann bestehende Gefahren erheblich verstärken. Eine gemeinsame Studie der Zurich Insurance Group und der Universität St. Gallen zeigt, weshalb solche Risiken für Versicherer zunehmend schwieriger kalkulierbar werden. Eine Studie der Zurich Insurance Group zeigt, weshalb KI Risiken für Versicherer zunehmend schwieriger kalkulierbar werden. (Bild: Shutterstock). Montag, 23. November 2026 09:00. Von Stefan Waldvogel | Redaktor. KI-Risiken könnten Versicherer an ihre Grenzen bringen. Je stärker Unternehmen künstliche Intelligenz (KI) in ihre Geschäftsprozesse integrieren, desto grösser wird die Gefahr, dass einzelne Fehler weitreichende Folgen haben. Im Extremfall könnten Schäden entstehen, welche die Kapazitäten des privaten Versicherungsmarktes übersteigen. Zu diesem Schluss kommt der Bericht «The AI Resilience Challenge», den die Zurich Insurance Group zusammen mit der Universität St. Gallen im Rahmen des Zurich AI Lab erarbeitet hat. Grundlage sind Interviews mit 50 Fachleuten, darunter 36 Führungskräfte und Spezialisten von Zurich sowie 14 externe Experten. Die Gespräche fanden zwischen Juli und September 2026 statt. Gemeinsame Abhängigkeiten als Gefahr. Eine zentrale Herausforderung sehen die Autoren in der zunehmenden Konzentration auf wenige Technologieanbieter. Unternehmen, die unterschiedliche KI-Anwendungen nutzen, können dennoch von denselben grundlegenden Modellen, Cloud-Infrastrukturen oder Datenquellen abhängig sein. Fällt ein solcher Anbieter aus oder wird ein gemeinsam genutztes System kompromittiert, können zahlreiche Unternehmen und ganze Branchen gleichzeitig betroffen sein. Als Beispiel für die Folgen technologischer Abhängigkeiten verweist die Studie auf den weltweiten IT-Ausfall im Jahr 2024. Ein fehlerhaftes Softwareupdate eines Cybersicherheitsanbieters legte rund 8,5 Millionen Geräte lahm und beeinträchtigte unter anderem Banken, Fluggesellschaften und Spitäler. Der Vorfall hatte zwar keinen direkten KI-Bezug, verdeutlicht aber die möglichen Auswirkungen gemeinsam genutzter Technologien. Gleichartige Fehler auch ohne gemeinsamen Anbieter. Noch schwieriger einzuschätzen sind Risiken, bei denen unterschiedliche KI-Systeme aufgrund ähnlicher Trainingsdaten, Entscheidungslogiken oder Zielsetzungen dieselben Fehler machen. Solche Zusammenhänge müssen nicht durch den Ausfall eines einzelnen Anbieters ausgelöst werden. Vielmehr können Fehlentscheidungen über längere Zeit in verschiedenen Unternehmen auftreten, ohne dass ihre gemeinsame Ursache unmittelbar erkennbar ist. Gerade für die Finanzbranche ist dies relevant. Nutzen Banken, Versicherer und Vermögensverwalter vergleichbare KI-Modelle zur Analyse oder Entscheidungsfindung, könnten sich Fehlentwicklungen über mehrere Institute hinweg verstärken. Vier Kategorien von KI-Risiken. Zur systematischen Einordnung unterscheidet die Studie vier Risikobereiche. Die erste Kategorie umfasst begrenzte, nachvollziehbare Schäden, die sich mit bestehenden Versicherungsprodukten grundsätzlich abdecken lassen. In der zweiten Kategorie stehen Risiken, deren Ursachen zwar erkennbar sind, die aber gleichzeitig zahlreiche Unternehmen treffen können. Die dritte Kategorie betrifft schwer nachvollziehbare Fehler, bei denen etwa Haftungsfragen oder Entscheidungswege ungeklärt bleiben. Die vierte Kategorie umfasst systemische Risiken mit potenziell weitreichenden Folgen, deren Umfang und Ursachen sich im Voraus kaum bestimmen lassen. Besonders kritisch wird es, wenn KI-Systeme eigenständig Verträge abschliessen, Dienstleistungen einkaufen oder Transaktionen ausführen. Für solche autonomen Anwendungen fehlen bislang ausreichende Erfahrungswerte über Häufigkeit und Ausmass möglicher Schäden. Grenzen der Versicherbarkeit.

title: AI-forward insurance startup Corgi applies for bank charter
summary: Corgi wants a national bank charter, which would put its holding company under the Federal Reserve’s purview – a rarity among insurance firms.
excerpt: An article from. AI-forward insurance startup Corgi applies for bank charter. Corgi wants a national bank charter, which would put its holding company under the Federal Reserve’s purview – a rarity among insurance firms. Published Nov. 23, 2026. Dan Ennis Senior Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. The fintech Corgi applied last week for a national bank charter with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The move marks the latest attempt at expansion for a 2-year-old artificial intelligence-powered insurance firm that has since diversified into exchange-traded funds. If approved, Corgi’s banking subsidiary would be based in Salt Lake City with loan production offices planned for San Francisco and New York. Corgi now serves roughly 300,000 insurance customers – mostly small-business owners, according to the company’s website. The type of charter Corgi has applied for represents a somewhat unique choice: It would force the insurer to become a bank holding company subject to Federal Reserve supervision. “That’s the kind of oversight nonbank financial firms, including insurers, left banking to avoid,” Victoria Baptiste, principal at consulting firm FS Vector, told American Banker. Roughly 45 insurance companies, between 1997 and 2000, applied to become thrifts, according to research from the University of North Carolina. That structure allowed parent firms to avoid becoming bank holding companies. Many insurance firms, however, left the banking space when the Dodd-Frank Act placed thrifts under the Fed’s purview. Corgi plans to offer checking and savings accounts, treasury services, credit cards, loans and lines of credit – options Baptiste calls “pretty traditional” in contrast to the company’s self-description as a “super intelligence-native” firm. “AI lets us do a lot where we can remove a lot of paperwork that wasn’t possible before, and that lets us make banking, as well as insurance, a lot more affordable,” Nicolas Laqua, Corgi’s CEO, told Bloomberg. But the firm’s proposed bank touts several executives with banking experience. Corgi has tapped Jason Wessling , who until August served as CEO of Oregon-based Pacific West Bank , to serve as the banking subsidiary’s president and CEO. ( FS Bancorp , for reference, completed its acquisition of Pacific West in August. ). Eric Vigil, who served until September as chief compliance officer at Austin, Texas-based American Bank, will be Corgi Bank’s compliance chief, according to his LinkedIn profile. Rudolph Garcia , a veteran chief credit officer at San Francisco-area lenders Altos Bank and Beacon Business Bank, is slated to serve as Corgi Bank’s credit chief. Corgi has also applied for deposit insurance with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. , according to a LinkedIn description from one of the proposed bank’s executives. “Corgi’s use of AI to drive down consumer costs will be an advantage in the review process, but the regulators will probe how the firm uses AI and whether it is well-controlled,” Roman Goldstein, a senior director at financial services advisory firm Klaros Group, told American Banker. Corgi plans to commit at least $75 million in initial capital to build its bank, Laqua said. The company had a private valuation of $4 billion as of June, according to a report from CB Insights. However, Bloomberg put Corgi’s value at roughly $7 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. Corgi raised about $450 million in its latest funding round, according to the company’s website. Add us on Google. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Ionic Wealth, the wealth management platform backed by stockbroker Angel One, has raised Rs 177 crore in a strategic funding round led by Angel One and a group of prominent business families. The latest investment takes the company’s total capital raised to approximately Rs 466 crore since it began operations in 2024. The Mumbai based wealth tech company plans to use the fresh funds to strengthen its investment offerings, integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into its platform, expand its ultra high net worth individual (UHNI) business and hire specialised professionals. It also plans to increase its presence in domestic and international markets. Ionic Wealth has reported assets under management (AUM) of more than Rs 16,000 crore as of September 2026. Its client base includes over 2,900 high net worth individuals (HNIs) and UHNIs across more than 12 cities. The company has a team of over 100 private bankers. The platform has recorded rapid growth since its launch. Its AUM increased from around Rs 3,800 crore in March 2025 to more than Rs 16,000 crore in September 2026. During the same period, its client base nearly quadrupled from approximately 680 to over 2,900. Founded in 2024 by Srikanth Subramanian, Shobhit Mathur and Dharmendra Jain, Ionic Wealth provides investment and wealth management services to affluent clients. Its offerings include portfolio management services, investment advisory and alternative investment funds. With the latest funding, the company aims to develop a dedicated wealth management proposition for India’s wealthiest families. It also plans to strengthen global investment opportunities through GIFT City and expand access to products under the Accredited Investor framework and Specialised Investment Funds.
